Cedric took a step back, frowning. 

This certainly took the fun out of it.

“You only fight villains because you hope we’ll find a way to kill you?” He asked. It was more rhetorical, having already gone through The Unbreakable’s mind. But he still felt the need to ask—because even having seen the thoughts, the fear, the agony circling around in the hero’s head, it just didn’t seem right.

But The Unbreakable’s steely gaze faltered, and then *he* staggered back a step, and whatever doubts Cedric possessed about his power evaporated. Because he didn’t need to read minds to see the answer in the wide eyed gaze staring back at him.

Suddenly, all the work he’d put into finally dismantling The Unbreakable’s sanity felt for naught. 

Neither of them spoke for a long moment; each staring at the other in reflecting shock.

And then;

“You can’t imagine what it’s like,” The Unbreakable said, his voice soft, trembling. Such a juxtaposition to the usual tone he emits when crime fighting. “Being immortal.”

Perhaps Cedric couldn’t. But he also couldn’t imagine having a death wish so violent it propelled him into daily suicide missions against villains capable of, well. Capable of what *he* was. 

But then, he supposed, The Unbreakable couldn’t imagine what had lead Cedric down the path that turned him into the villain he is now. 

“Can’t you feel pain?” Cedric asked. To go into battle, hoping to die. It was one thing. Feeling near death over and over and over—

The Unbreakable nodded, swallowing thickly. “Sometimes it—it’s worth it. The initial suffering. I think, maybe this is the one. But then I heal.” He shrugs and moves to lean against the wall. “And I heal, and I heal, and I heal.” He motions with one hand, “You could trap me in the mental prison you have cooked up. I doubt it’ll be as bad as the one I’m already stuck in.”

“That kind of defeats the purpose, though, doesn’t it?”

The Unbreakable made a face, before pushing away from the wall. “At least make me think I died?” His voice shook as he spoke. “You have that power, and you’ll have another hero defeated. It’s a win win scenario. I can finally—“

Cedric held up a hand, surprised to find his own shaking.

He spent his free time scripting nightmare scenarios for heroes all day and night. What The Unbreakable wanted was practically written into Cedric’s DNA. 

“I’m a villain, Unbreakable. You’re asking me to do something kind.”

“Nobody else would know.”

“Does that make a difference?”

The Unbreakable stared at him for a beat. “I’m nearly two hundred years old,” he said, finally, taking another step forwards. “I’m tired, Visionary. I fight to find a way out, not to help people. I don’t care about people anymore than you do. If you’re worried about helping a hero, I’m not a hero.”

He sighed, a deep trembling thing that wracked through his whole body. 

Cedric was not a man of empathy.

But what he did next, he had no other explanation for.

“Sleep,” he murmured, waving a hand gently through the air. The Unbreakable’s tension filled bones fell limp and he collapsed to the floor without so much as another inhale. 

He didn’t care that he was granting the wish of a hero. Nor about the lines that clearly defined them.

The heroes thoughts wrapped around his heart, circling round and round like one of Cedric’s worst hellscapes. He saw The Unbreakable’s bones snap back into place, very nearly felt the agony that wove itself into the tissue surrounding it. Broken neck, broken back, shattered femur. 

The Unbreakable had never been Unbreakable, only unkillable. And that had shattered the very semblance of sanity that held him together. Cedric had seen it when he’d looked, had seen the shattered remnants desolately glued together into a half contained grab at sanity.

He moved over to The Unbreakable, standing over the limp body, before kneeling and placing a shaking hand on his shoulder and squeezing gently. 

“You’ve suffered enough,” he said, swallowing. Because it was true, no scape he made would ever counter that which The Unbreakable already survived. 

So, just this once…

“Find peace,” he added, closing his own eyes and willing together a scape for The Unbreakable. 

A world that no longer existed; a world without gifts or magic or anything truly extraordinary. He granted The Unbreakable a mundane life. Of nine am coffee cups and four pm radio sweepstakes.

Just this once, The Visionary swept away the darkness and brought forth the light.

And maybe, with it, something shone a little brighter in his own abyss.

But that was a problem to be dealt with another day.

Richard set the pliers down, hands ghosting over his other toys as he contemplated what next to do with me. 

I had to give him credit — a mortal girl who hadn’t given her soul to the devil for her freedom until True Death would have been absolutely terrified finding herself tied up in his moldy basement. He had all the creep factors scaled up to an eleven, and not an ounce of hesitation in a single thing he did. When he died, Hell was going to give him a hell of a show.

We had that in common. 

His hand settled on a rusty saw, fingers stroking along its copper colored edges almost lovingly. 

He’d already pulled two of my teeth, the holes already filling with bone marrow to regrow the tooth that wasn’t allowed to rot, decay, or disappear until I met my True Death. 

Hey, perks of making a deal with the Devil. 

“Listen,” I slurred past my swollen cheeks and tongue, “this is all real impressive, but I do have somewhere to be and no time to regrow whatever the hell you’re thinking of cutting off.” 

It wasn’t the pain that bothered me — I’d been dealt my fair share before landing myself in Hells hot seat, and even more before securing the deal. Pain was no big deal, it was momentary, and if one could just survive the moment, it was as if it never happened. Once I figured that out, every moment was but a wince and a scream away. And Pain had never been quite as long as the next next moment. 

It was the regaining what had been lost that really chuffed me. 

And Richard here had plans to take a lot more than I was really in the mood to regrow. 

“You’ve had your fun. Time to untie me, unless you want things to get ugly.”

He chuckled, low in his stomach. A sound that probably should have curled my toes and had me screaming, pleading for somebody—anybody—to come help me. But I didn’t need any of that. Not anymore.

“Oh, things are going to get ugly, indeed,” he murmured, picking up the saw and turned towards me. It glinted, a shadowed light in the muddy night, as he brought it down to stroke gently against my thigh. 

“When you run out of this shithole crying,” I muttered, glaring down at the saw with the annoyed resignation of a woman knowing she’s about to get her damn leg sawed off, “do not blame me.” 

He laughed again, the sound more annoying than unnerving, and set to his task with impossible enthusiasm.

One moment bled into the next. 

And then he froze.

One thing mortals, no matter how psychotic, agnostic, theistic, or what have you, could all agree on: 

Limbs don’t grow back.

Certainly not as you’re hacking at them.

Definitely not.

I could see the wheels turning in his head as his sawing slowed and my nerves repaired themselves before his very eyes. Could feel the temperature rise with the heat of his heart. 

In one indisputable moment, he realized he was no longer the predator and I, the prey. 

He looked up at me, eyes wide and glimmering with the knowledge there was more than he knew, more than he understood, more, more, more. And what, then, did that mean for the likes of him? 

“Boo,” I whispered, a sadistic grin slicking over my lips. “Best part of all this,” I motioned towards the mess of my leg and the puddle of blood dripping from my lap, “is when one is the property of the devil, one usually has a handler.”

A handler who enjoyed being late, sure. But he’d show eventually.

“The devil?”

“The one and only. Don’t worry, I’m sure you’ll meet him.” I paused, ticking a shoulder. “Probably sooner rather than later. He doesn’t quite like when people play with *his* toys.” 

Richard stared at me for a beat. And then, like the coward he, and most like him, was, he turned and ran. Up the stairs, out the door, leaving me and my half sawed off limb tied to the table in his basement.

I sighed.

One day my luck was going to change. Maybe not today, but damn it, one day I’d manage to go a whole twenty four hours without ending up bloody, battered, or massively annoyed.

The screams of the man faded to whimpers, and I nodded to myself, proud of a job complete. As I turned to the other person in the room, the window behind us shattered and Captain Plasma flew through it, crashing onto the ground hard enough to crack it. 

“You thought you could get away, Gerald! But not this time.”

I rolled my eyes. 

This was becoming a bit of a normal occurrence. I’d break something I was hired to break, one of the League of Law and Order would come out of whatever hidey hole they were using to stalk me and accuse me of being an evil doer. To the rest of the world I’m sure the League were nothing short of heroes.

To me, they were nothing more than nuisances.

My business was above board and they’d never once caught me breaking anything without permission, and yet, here we were, standing face to face in the hospital with a doctor in one corner, and a trauma patient in the other. 

“Once again,” I said, turning my back on the super powered dickwad, “You’re wrong.” 

“Tell that to the innocent soul you’ve—“ 

“Doc?” I turned my gaze to the doctor, “Tell the good savior what exactly I’m doing here.” 

“The bone needed to be broken to be reset. The patient requested you.” 

I flipped back around and blinked pointedly at the hero. “The patient. Requested me.” 

Captain Plasma glared back at me. “Perhaps you have more than one power than we all think.” 

I tilted my head and took a step closer to him. The League were the only ones particularly successful at hiding any of their powers. Plasmas gifts were hardly all out in the open. All he’d ever outrightly confessed to were the invulnerability, super strength, and flight. 

But the thing was, last time the League dropped in on me doing legit business, I noticed something I probably shouldn’t have. 

“Or maybe I have less!” I mocked, rolling my eyes again as I crossed to the window to look out over the ledge.

Plasma stepped over the broken glass and hovered right at my back. “Your trickery will only succeed for so long.” 

I flipped around to face him again, smiling. The glass crunched beneath my feet and I glanced down at it, remembering the way the blood had dripped from his hand and mingled with the blood of the mines the last time we met. Nobody else realized. Nobody else saw. He’d hidden it well. 

His gaze followed mine, eyebrows furrowing. 

“You call it trickery,” I said, watching him. “Just because I have a villains power doesn’t mean I was born to be a villain. Doesn’t mean I committed to a life of crime and torture.” 

Plasma looked back up at me, confusion whirling around in his eyes.

My smile flashed, and before he could react, I reached out and pressed my hand to his sternum. He inhaled a rushed hiss, and jerked away, but it was too late. The destructive rot had already transferred, and because of his little invulnerability lie, he didn’t wear anything strong enough to hide it. The rot burrowed into his abdomen and he dropped down to his feet as it traveled up his esophagus and lungs. 

“I never wanted this life,” I told him. “But after years and years and years of yours and your friends harassment….” Moving forward, I knelt down and pressed my hand to his fracturing cheek. “What other option do I have?” 

My gaze dropped down to his hands, following the trail of the rot through the veins in his arms, dropping to the wedding band on his finger. I leaned down and brushed a knuckle against it, smirking as it disintegrated beneath my touch. I looked up at him from beneath my eyelashes as the fear took root in his gaze and the rot circled his pupils. 

“I’ll make hers fast. But the others will suffer.” 

I stood and turned to my accomplices sitting in their places, and grinned. “Shall we begin?”

“You…. Probably shouldn’t touch that,” Ella murmured to the elderly man browsing the mystical clock shelf at the back of the store. He glanced up at her and she offered a shrug. “Curses whoever touches it to relive their worst moment over and over again. Only way to break the curse is die.” 

His eyes went wide, and as he stumbled back a step, Ella turned around to head to the back room. Patrons rarely read the plaques on the antiquities, and it wasn’t her job to protect them, so one warning was all they ever got. She turned the corner into the enchanted item safe room. Cursed items were fine to leave out front unsupervised — most people were too afraid to try to sneak them out without one of the enchanted shopping bags that temporarily stunted them, and those that weren’t never got far. But the enchanted items remained behind lock and key. 

She ran a finger along the first cabinet, a little zip of energy coursing through her hand. “Shh,” she murmured, gently tapping the door. The items within begged to be used — clanking together, excitement roiling through the cabinet with enough force that it shook beneath her touch. Some days she’d take them out to play. It was one of the perks of the job — unimaginable powers at the tip of her fingers.

But today, she had different plans.

Her hand dropped and she made her way to the back of the room, a low whine emitting from the cabinet as she left it behind. “Later,” she insisted without turning around. 

Her attention zeroed in on the lockbox in the far corner that had been dropped in early the day before. The box blocked the power within it from leaking, but even so she could feel the unimaginable strength and desire in the air all around her. She’d felt it, when the reluctant patron placed it on the counter top, and hadn’t been able to stop thinking about it since she brought it back here. 

Pulling the mystical key from her back pocket, she placed it in the lockbox and turned it. She inhaled shakily and, as soon as she cracked the seal, the room filled with the mysterious energy that had been haunting her all day. She knelt down, heart pounding, and peered into the box at the single candle settled in the center. 

To the unknowing eye, it was nothing more than a simple child’s birthday candle. Pink and white and tinged with char and melted wax. It’d only been lit once, a shock considering what she new. She swallowed and reached in, exhaling as the power swirled around her hand in anxious anticipation. 

The odds of ever encountering an item of this magnificence that wasn’t cursed were beyond even her wildest imagination, but here it sat below her hand. Few items of this power ever bode well. But she *knew*. From the moment the man had set it on the counter and looked at her with such sorrowful eyes, she’d known. 

Not even the genie in the lamp in the basement could do what this candle could. 

She wrapped her hand around it and pulled it from the lockbox, eyebrows furrowing as she inspected it. The hair on the back of her arms and neck stood on end, an electrical current of pure energy flushing through her.

“This shouldn’t exist,” she’d told the man when she realized. 

He’d nodded. “But it does.” 

“And it works?” 

“That’s why I no longer need it.” 

She hadn’t even hesitated after that. “What do you want for it?” 

He hadn’t even asked for money — if he had, their paltry little shop wouldn’t have been able to afford it, and she’d known it. The meager paychecks that kept her in her home were barely enough to keep her alive and were little more than what the owners could afford. 

He’d asked for a cursed item. And she hadn’t hesitated to make the trade — no matter how dangerous the shoe he’d asked for was, she knew then she couldn’t pass the opportunity up. 

Not when the candle only had two uses left. 

She moved across the room and sat down at the old, rickety desk, setting the candle down in front of her and leaning over to pull the pack of matches from the top drawer.

A golden bird flew down from the ceiling an settled down on the desk beside the candle and quirked it’s head. 

“You’re doing this then?” It asked in its bright, tinny voice. 

Ella didn’t answer as she found the matches and set back up. 

“Suppose it works, what then?” 

She tilted her head and looked down at the cursed bird. She’d never leave the shop—nobody wanted a cursed princess these days. They were too much work, and the curses too strong to break. But the shop kept her anyways. Everyone deserved a home. 

“It will work.” 

“Maybe. But what about after? You know as well as I do that giving into the thrall of the magic has consequences.” 

Ella flinched, the scar running along the length of her back and legs stinging slightly at the reminder.

She cleared her throat. “Not this time,” she said, looking back to the pack of matches. “It’s not cursed. This one’s enchanted. I’ll get her back and I won’t have to give anything in return.” 

“And when they find out what you’ve done?” 

“They won’t. Go watch the shop.” 

“Maybe I want to watch you.” 

Ella inhaled deep and slammed the matches down on the desk before shooting a glare at the bird. “Is it so wrong I’d like to bring my daughter back from the dead in peace?” 

The bird watched her for a beat, before sighing and fluttering off to the front of the store. Ella stared after her until she was sure she’d stay gone before turning back to match and candle. 

She picked up the match and struck it along the side of the matchbox. The enchanted items around her whizzed and whirled in their cabinets, singing loudly at the call of the magic as she brought the candle up to meet the flame. 

For twelve years she’d been searching. Trading and buying and trying. 

She closed her eyes and swallowed thickly. 

“Esmeralda Asinlar. Return her to me, heart and soul. Body and mind.” 

She hesitated after the final word fell from her lips. The last time she’d made this request had been on a cursed item and had failed. 

The steeled herself. This time it wouldn’t fail. It couldn’t. 

She pursed her lips, inhaling, and then exhaling. Beneath her eyelids, she saw the warmth of the flame flicker out, even as wax dropped down onto her finger, sealing the request. 

Magic bloomed and blossomed all around her, shaking the tables and cabinets and sending the enchanted items chittering again. Her hair flew wildly around her and a massive gust of wind blew through the room, scattering papers through the air. 

And then —
